limitations: It does not check facts. It can tell you a page is commission-funded and that other sources disagree, not whether a stated rate or figure is real.
Stance is keyword matching over a search snippet, not a reading of the page. It misses sarcasm, conditionals and comparisons, and abstains often by design.
Everything is read from search titles, snippets and URLs. Conflicts of interest that don't show there (a disclosure further down the page, a link added by script) are invisible.
The domain list is hand-curated, finite and English/Korean-leaning. Unlisted sites count as unknown, so claims about regional products mostly reflect Meika's ignorance of the sources.
Brand matching compares claim words with the site's domain name. It misses brands whose domain doesn't contain the name and can fire on generic words.
Echo collapse catches republication of the same text, not coordinated campaigns in different words.
Guarantees and predictions about the future can't be settled by any source, so they always carry the full unfalsifiability penalty.

Personal context is this month's spending, your budget and (if you entered it) your savings. Meika doesn't know your income, debts or portfolio, so this is decision support, not a suitability assessment.
Search results change over time and by country; each evaluation freezes the evidence it used.
Every threshold is an argued design choice, not fitted to outcomes (there is no ground truth for 'was this worth acting on'), so the score is not calibrated.
English lexicons only: a claim in Korean will mostly be unclassified and most sources will read as neutral.
disclaimer: This is a caution score, not a truth score. Meika does not fact-check claims; it weighs where the claim's support comes from and what acting on it would mean for your budget. This is not financial advice.
